analogy.p: Think of the digital divide as a town where some streets have a bus to the library and other streets do not: those with the bus can borrow books, learn skills and apply for jobs, while others fall behind unless the council builds new routes or opens a mobile library. Privacy is like the town's CCTV and loyalty cards: they record where you go and what you borrow. That can help catch thieves or offer you better recommendations, but it is only acceptable if people know what is recorded, who can see it and that it is locked away safely. The analogy breaks down because digital data can be copied endlessly and sent worldwide in a second, and a digital 'bus route' needs both a connection and the skills to use it.
analogy.t: A town's library card and its CCTV

bullets: The **digital divide** is the gap between people who have access to digital technology and those who do not.
**Privacy** is a person's right to control who collects, uses and sees information about them.
You may be asked to **describe, explain or discuss** an impact, giving benefits and drawbacks for the stakeholders.
Typical questions: reasons for the divide, effects on a group of people, ways of reducing it, how a technology affects privacy and how data can be protected.
Link to 1.6.2 legislation (Data Protection Act 2018), 1.4 security (encryption, passwords, data breaches) and 1.6.1 stakeholders.
Both issues can be placed under **ethical**, **cultural** and **legal** headings, which helps you structure a longer answer.
core.p: This point sits within OCR J277 1.6.1 (impacts of digital technology on wider society) and asks you to understand two linked issues: the **digital divide** and **privacy**. You should be able to explain what the digital divide is, who it affects and why it matters, and to explain how digital technology threatens personal privacy and how individuals and organisations can protect it. Both topics are examined through scenarios, so you must apply them to schools, hospitals, shops, councils and social media rather than just recall definitions.

bullets: Three parts to the divide: **access** (devices and connection), **affordability** (cost of equipment and data) and **ability** (digital skills and confidence).
It exists **within** a country (for example between rich and poor households) and **between** countries (developed and developing).
It is a **cultural** and **ethical** issue because it affects fairness and equal opportunity.
The divide is not fixed: it can widen if technology changes faster than some groups can keep up, or narrow with investment and training.
Also called digital exclusion for those who are left out.
Link: the more services that are 'digital by default', the more important it is to close the divide.
core.p: The **digital divide** is the **gap between people, groups or countries that have access to digital technology (computers, smartphones, the internet) and the skills to use it, and those that do not**. It is not just about owning a device. Access can mean reliable, fast and affordable internet; **skills** can mean knowing how to use technology safely and effectively. A person with a phone but no home broadband, or without the confidence to use online services, can still be on the wrong side of the divide. As more education, banking, shopping, government and health services move online, being excluded becomes a bigger disadvantage.

bullets: **Low income / cost**: devices, software and broadband subscriptions are expensive, and some families cannot afford them.
**Geography**: rural and remote areas often have poor or no broadband and weak mobile signal because it is costly to install infrastructure there.
**Age**: some older people did not grow up with technology and may lack confidence or skills.
**Disability**: websites or devices that are not accessible (for example without screen readers or captions) exclude some users.
**Education and skills**: people who have never been taught how to use technology safely cannot benefit from it.
**Language and culture**: much online content is in a few languages, so others are excluded.
**Developing countries**: limited infrastructure, electricity and wealth restrict access for whole populations.
**Attitude and awareness**: some people do not see the benefit or fear scams and so avoid the internet.
core.p: There are several overlapping reasons why some people lack access or skills. Often a person is affected by more than one at the same time, which makes the divide harder to close. When you write about causes, always say **why** the factor leads to exclusion, for example 'low income means a family cannot afford a laptop or monthly broadband, so children cannot complete online homework'.

bullets: **Education**: pupils without a computer or internet struggle with homework and online learning, so may fall behind.
**Employment**: job vacancies and applications are mainly online, and many jobs require digital skills, so excluded people have fewer chances.
**Public services and health**: booking appointments, benefits, tax and council services online may be hard for those without access.
**Cost**: online deals, price comparison and internet banking are often cheaper, so those offline may pay more.
**Social isolation**: communication with family and friends increasingly uses messaging and video calls.
**Economic inequality** between regions and countries can widen because businesses and trade depend on digital connections.
**Democratic participation**: less access to news and information can affect how informed people are.
Positive side: access to technology can raise living standards and give people in remote places a voice and new markets.
core.p: The divide matters because **opportunities increasingly depend on being online**. People on the wrong side can find it harder to learn, find work, get cheaper deals, access public services and stay in touch. This can make existing inequalities worse: those who already have less are further disadvantaged, while those with access gain more. Linking an effect to a particular stakeholder, such as a pupil, a job seeker or a pensioner, makes your answer specific.

bullets: **Public access**: free computers and Wi-Fi in libraries, community centres and schools.
**Investment in infrastructure**: extending broadband and mobile coverage to rural areas.
**Affordable options**: social tariffs, low-cost devices and schemes that lend or donate refurbished equipment.
**Education and training**: digital skills classes for older people and adults, and teaching technology in schools.
**Accessible design**: following accessibility standards (text size, screen reader support, captions, simple layouts).
**Keeping offline alternatives** such as phone lines or paper forms for essential services.
**Reuse of old devices**: donating working equipment links to the e-waste topic.
Evaluation: these help, but cost money, take time and do not remove all barriers such as lack of confidence.
core.p: The divide can be reduced by **governments, schools, businesses and charities** working together to improve access, affordability and skills. A good answer links each action to the cause it tackles, such as providing free internet access in libraries for people who cannot afford home broadband. You may also be asked to discuss whether such measures are enough, and who should pay for them.

bullets: **Personal data** is information that can identify a living person.
Privacy matters because data can be **stolen, sold, combined or misused**, and once online it is hard to remove.
Loss of privacy can cause **identity theft, fraud, stalking, discrimination or embarrassment**.
People often exchange privacy for **convenience** (free apps in return for data), sometimes without realising.
Privacy rights are strongest when people give **informed consent**: they know what is collected, why and for how long.
Organisations have a duty to keep the data **secure** and only use it for the stated purpose.
The balance: public safety measures (CCTV, monitoring) versus individuals' right not to be watched.
core.h: What privacy means and why it matters
core.p: **Privacy** is about a person's ability to **keep information about themselves under their own control** and to avoid being watched or tracked without agreeing to it. Personal data such as names, addresses, photographs, health records, browsing history and location can be used to help us, for example by recommending useful services, but also to harm us through fraud, discrimination or unwanted targeting. Privacy is both an **ethical** matter (do people have a right to be left alone?) and a **legal** one (the Data Protection Act 2018 sets rules). The challenge is balancing privacy against benefits such as security and convenience.

bullets: **Cookies**: small text files stored by a website in the browser. Some are useful (remembering a basket or login); **third-party cookies** track browsing across sites to build advertising profiles.
**Location tracking**: phones, apps and fitness devices record where a person goes, which can reveal their home, work and routines.
**Social media**: posts, photos and 'likes' reveal personal details and may be seen by employers, strangers or criminals if privacy settings are open.
**CCTV and facial recognition**: record people in public spaces and can identify them automatically.
**Smart devices** (speakers, TVs, doorbells) may record audio or video and send it to company servers.
**Data breaches**: hackers steal databases of names, passwords and payment details from organisations.
**Data sharing and selling**: companies may pass your data to third parties, often described in long terms and conditions that few people read.
**Phishing and scams** use personal details gathered online to appear convincing.
core.p: Modern technology collects data constantly and cheaply, often in the background. Because information can be **copied, stored indefinitely and combined** with other data, a few harmless-seeming details can build a detailed picture of someone's habits, interests and location. Learn a range of examples and be ready to explain how each one reduces privacy and who benefits.

bullets: Under UK rules, websites should explain which non-essential cookies they use and ask for **consent**.
Users can **accept, reject or manage** cookie choices and can delete cookies in browser settings.
**Private (incognito) browsing** does not save history or cookies locally after the session, but it does not make you anonymous to the website or your internet provider.
Tracking makes advertising more relevant and funds free services (benefit), but reduces privacy (drawback).
**Metadata** such as time, location and device type can reveal a lot even without the content of messages.
Link to Data Protection Act 2018: personal data collected through cookies must be handled lawfully and fairly.
core.h: Cookies and online tracking in more detail
core.p: A **cookie** is a small file that a website asks your browser to store so it can recognise you on later visits. A **session cookie** lasts only while you are on the site, and a **persistent cookie** remains for a set period. **First-party cookies** come from the site you are visiting and mostly make it work properly (for example keeping items in a shopping basket). **Third-party cookies** come from another company, often an advertising network whose content appears on many sites, so the same identifier can be seen on each one and used to build a profile of your interests. This is why a product you looked at can appear in adverts elsewhere.

bullets: Use **privacy settings** on social media so only friends can see posts and photos.
Create **strong, unique passwords** and use two-step verification where possible.
Think before sharing: avoid posting **location, address, school or holiday plans** publicly.
Read **permissions and terms** before installing apps; deny access to contacts, camera or location that is not needed.
Manage or reject **non-essential cookies** and clear browsing data.
Use **encrypted** connections (HTTPS) and keep software updated and **anti-malware** installed.
Be alert to **phishing** emails and messages asking for personal details.
Use **public Wi-Fi** carefully because other users on the network may be able to intercept unencrypted data.
core.h: Protecting your privacy: what individuals can do
core.p: Individuals can take sensible steps to **reduce the amount of personal data they give away and to keep it secure**. No single measure is perfect, so exam answers should show a combination and explain why each one helps. Link each method to the threat it reduces, for example strong, unique passwords reduce the chance of someone gaining access to an account.

bullets: Collect only the data that is **needed** and keep it **no longer than necessary**.
Obtain **consent** and be clear about what data is used for.
Use **encryption**, firewalls, access levels and strong authentication to keep data secure.
Report **data breaches** and tell affected people.
Allow individuals to **see, correct and request deletion** of their data in line with their rights.
**Anonymise** data where possible so it cannot be linked to a person.
Train staff so they do not leak data by mistake or fall for phishing.
**Fines and legal action** encourage organisations to take privacy seriously.
core.h: Protecting privacy: what organisations and the law do
core.p: Organisations that hold personal data have **legal and ethical responsibilities** to protect it. In the UK this is set out mainly in the **Data Protection Act 2018** (the UK's version of GDPR), which gives people rights over their data and requires organisations to handle it lawfully, fairly and securely. The Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) enforces the law and can fine organisations that misuse data or fail to protect it. Good practice also includes staff training and security technology.

bullets: **For data collection**: crime prevention, safety, convenience, personalised services, medical research, free apps.
**Against data collection**: loss of control, risk of breaches, discrimination, constant monitoring, commercial exploitation.
**Proportionality**: data collection should be reasonable for its purpose (for example CCTV in public areas but not in changing rooms).
**Consent** and transparency make collection more acceptable.
**Stakeholders** to name: individuals, companies, employers, the public and the state.
A strong conclusion states the safeguards that would make the collection acceptable.
Link to the digital divide: people with less digital literacy may be less able to manage their privacy settings.
core.p: Privacy is rarely absolute: there are good reasons to collect data, such as keeping people safe or providing a personalised service. The skill examiners reward is **weighing the competing interests of different stakeholders**. A hospital sharing patient data can improve care and research, but must protect confidentiality. CCTV in a town centre can deter crime, but also records innocent people. Decide which interest should win in the situation given and justify it.

bullets: Programmes that teach **digital skills** should include online safety and privacy.
Public computers and Wi-Fi help close the divide but need security measures such as logging out and avoiding saving passwords.
Older or less confident users may be targeted by **phishing** and **fraud**.
Access to technology brings **both benefits and risks**, so the aim is safe, equal access.
Organisations should design services that are **accessible, simple and secure**.
This links to the broader 1.6.1 theme: the same technology produces different effects for different stakeholders.
core.h: Linking the digital divide and privacy
core.p: The two issues interact. People who lack digital skills are often **less aware of privacy risks** and may be more vulnerable to scams or to sharing too much data. At the same time, services that require people to go online, such as banking and health, mean that those who have to use shared or public computers face extra privacy risks. Pointing out links like this shows examiners a high level of understanding and is useful in longer discussion answers.

exam: **State** (1 mark): give one precise answer, e.g. 'low income' as a cause of the digital divide or 'cookies' as a way of tracking.
**Define** digital divide (1 to 2 marks): 'the gap between those who have access to digital technology and those who do not', adding skills and affordability earns the second mark.
**Describe** (2 marks): a point plus detail, e.g. 'Rural areas may have poor broadband (1) because it is expensive to install cables (1)'.
**Explain** (2 to 4 marks): use 'because' to link cause and effect; each developed reason earns marks.
**Give two ways to reduce the digital divide** (2 to 4 marks): choose different types (infrastructure, training, public access) and say how each helps.
**Give two ways to protect your privacy** (2 marks): strong password and privacy settings are safe choices; add what each prevents.
**Discuss** (6 marks): balance benefits and drawbacks for named stakeholders, apply to the scenario, and give a conclusion.
Always **use the context**: if the scenario is a school, say pupils, parents and teachers, not 'people'.
Link to **laws** when relevant: the Data Protection Act 2018 makes organisations responsible for keeping data secure.
Avoid vague words like 'bad' or 'hack'; say 'data could be stolen in a breach' or 'unauthorised access'.
Use both **ethical** and **legal** vocabulary to show breadth, but develop only the points that fit.
Check the **mark allocation**: two marks means two distinct points, not one point repeated.

mistakes.r: It covers access, affordability and skills, including reliable internet and the ability to use technology safely.
mistakes.w: The digital divide only means not owning a computer.

mistakes.r: It exists within countries too, for example between rural and urban areas and between age groups.
mistakes.w: Saying the divide only affects poor countries.

mistakes.r: Explain barriers: cost of devices and broadband, lack of infrastructure, lack of skills or confidence.
mistakes.w: Writing 'people can just buy a computer'.

mistakes.r: Privacy is the right to control how personal information is collected and used, which includes consent.
It only stops local history and cookies being saved; websites and internet providers can still see activity.
mistakes.w: Saying incognito mode makes you anonymous.

mistakes.r: Some cookies are useful (basket, login); third-party tracking cookies are the privacy concern.
mistakes.w: Writing that all cookies are bad.

mistakes.r: State that it requires organisations to handle personal data lawfully, fairly and securely and gives individuals rights.
mistakes.w: Naming the Data Protection Act without saying what it does.

mistakes.r: Give benefits (safety, crime prevention) and drawbacks (loss of privacy), then conclude.
mistakes.w: Giving one-sided answers about CCTV or tracking.

mistakes.r: Match each action to the problem, e.g. free library Wi-Fi tackles lack of affordable access.
mistakes.w: Suggesting a solution without linking it to the cause.

summary: This point covers the digital divide (the gap between those with and without access to digital technology and the skills to use it) and privacy (control over personal data), including causes, effects, solutions and protections. It matters because Paper 1 scenario questions ask you to explain and discuss these impacts for different stakeholders.

terms.d: The gap between those who have access to digital technology and the skills to use it, and those who do not.
Being unable to take part fully in society because of a lack of access to or skills with digital technology.
Having the devices and a reliable, affordable internet connection needed to use digital services.
The knowledge and confidence needed to use technology effectively and safely.
The right of an individual to control information about themselves and to be free from unwanted observation.
Information that can identify a living person, such as a name, address, photograph, IP address or location.
A small text file stored by a browser at a website's request, used to recognise or track a user.
A cookie set by a company other than the site being visited, often used to track users across sites for advertising.
Freely given, informed agreement from a person to the collection or use of their data.
An incident in which personal data is accessed, stolen or released without authorisation.
The close monitoring of people, for example by CCTV, facial recognition or tracking software.
Using someone else's personal details to commit fraud or obtain goods and services.
Scrambling data so that it cannot be understood without the key, helping to keep it private.
UK law that controls how organisations use personal data and gives individuals rights over their data.
Fake emails or messages designed to trick people into revealing personal details.
Remove identifying details from data so that it cannot be linked to an individual.

worked.ans: Residents without good broadband cannot reach services (1) so may miss payments (1). Older residents may lack digital skills (1) and become excluded or be targeted by scams (1). The council could provide free computer sessions and training in the local library (1).
worked.q: A village has poor broadband and many older residents. The council moves all its services online. Explain two effects this could have on residents and suggest one way the council could reduce them. [5 marks]
steps: Effect 1: residents with no or slow broadband cannot access forms or pay bills (1), so they may miss deadlines or pay more (1).
Effect 2: older residents may lack digital skills or confidence (1), so they may feel excluded or fall victim to online scams (1).
Solution: offer free computer access and training in the library or keep phone and paper options (1).

worked.ans: A third-party cookie is placed by an advertising company (1) and recognises the same browser on many sites (1), allowing a profile of the user's interests to be built and used for targeted adverts (1).
worked.q: Describe how third-party cookies can reduce a person's privacy. [3 marks]
steps: Third-party cookies are set by a company other than the site visited, often an advertiser (1).
The same cookie identifier is recognised on many different websites (1).
The company can build up a profile of the person's browsing and interests, which is used for targeted advertising without the person always being aware (1).

worked.ans: Model answer: Facial recognition would help to deter theft and help police to identify offenders, which benefits shop owners and makes shoppers feel safer. However, it records every visitor, including innocent shoppers, and stores biometric personal data, so there is a risk that it could be hacked or misused and some people may be wrongly identified. The centre must follow the Data Protection Act 2018, which means displaying signs, keeping the footage secure and not keeping it longer than necessary. Overall, it can be justified if used proportionately with these safeguards, because the reduction in crime must be balanced against the right to privacy.
worked.q: A shopping centre plans to use CCTV with facial recognition to reduce theft. Discuss the privacy issues and the benefits. [6 marks]
steps: Benefits: deters and detects theft, helps police identify offenders, makes shoppers and staff feel safer.
Privacy issues: records everyone including innocent shoppers, stores biometric personal data, may be hacked or misused, may misidentify people.
Law and ethics: must follow the Data Protection Act 2018, tell people they are being filmed and keep the data secure and only for as long as needed.
Stakeholders: shoppers, staff, shop owners and police.
Conclusion: acceptable if proportionate, signs are displayed and data is protected; otherwise the loss of privacy outweighs the benefit.
